blogs.title: What Does It Mean to “Certify” Without a Signature? The Fifth Circuit’s Textual Turn in Williams v. GoAuto
blogs.description: The panel squarely rejects a signature requirement for premium-finance cancellation certifications under La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550(G)(3)(a), reading the statute’s use of “certifying” to permit company-level attestations without a named individual or autograph. This post unpacks the court’s textual reasoning, distinguishes Benitez v. Elsayed, and explores how corporate certifications, ESIGN/UETA-era practices, and records management intersect with Louisiana’s strict-compliance regime. We assess practical drafting tips for premium finance companies and insurers now that unsigned, entity-level certifications are judicially blessed—at least in federal court.

blogs.title: When an API Counts as a Mailroom: “Receipt” in the Age of Automated Cancellations
blogs.description: Williams resolves a pivotal ambiguity in § 9:3550(G)(3)(b)(i): what qualifies as insurer “receipt” of a cancellation request. Leaning on Black’s definitions and industry reality, the court holds that electronic delivery to, and automated processing by, GoAuto’s web service sufficed. This post analyzes the opinion’s embrace of machine-to-machine communications as legal ‘receipt,’ the implications for system design and audit trails, and potential vulnerabilities (system downtime, misrouted messages, proof burdens) that litigants should anticipate. We also note the court’s decision to sidestep the district court’s adventurous “private carrier” theory.

blogs.title: Strict Compliance, Modern Methods: Reconciling Louisiana’s Cancellation Formalism with Digital Workflows
blogs.description: Louisiana courts demand strict adherence for financed-policy cancellations, with any defect rendering cancellation ineffective. Williams affirms that principle while refusing to graft extra-statutory formalities (like signatures) and accepting electronic ‘receipt.’ This post examines the doctrinal tension between rigid compliance and flexible implementation, compares the decision to cases like Delatte, Eaglin, Britten, and Hodges, and offers a roadmap for litigants arguing whether “strict” means hyper-formalism or faithful textual adherence. We consider how plaintiffs might still attack cancellations post-Williams (timing, content, proof of insured notice, interested-party copies) despite the ruling.

blogs.title: No Certification to Baton Rouge: The Fifth Circuit’s Erie Guess and the Path for Future State-Court Clarification
blogs.description: The court declines to certify unsettled questions about “certifying” and “receipt” to the Louisiana Supreme Court, citing its general reluctance absent a compelling reason. This post situates that move within Fifth Circuit certification practice, weighs comity and forum-shopping concerns in class litigation over mass cancellation procedures, and forecasts how state appellate courts might treat Williams. We outline strategies for parties seeking definitive state-law rulings (parallel state actions, targeted interlocutory appeals) and the circumstances that might finally prompt certification in a future, factually messier case.
